item.title: From Coolum Beach to Netflix
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: The Sunshine Coast is set to reach millions of viewers around the world with the new Netflix feature film Allen […]
item.content:encoded:
The Sunshine Coast is set to reach millions of viewers around the world with the new Netflix feature film Allen launching globally on 12 November.

Filmed across South East Queensland, including key scenes shot at Mount Coolum, the Coolum Boardwalk, Coolum Beach and First Bay, Allen continues a growing list of screen productions choosing the Sunshine Coast as a backdrop.

With a premier screening in Brisbane on 11 November, the movie marks the third production in recent years to showcase the region’s distinctive landscapes, following the success of The Edge streamed on Netflix and Black Snow – Season 2, both seen by audiences around Australia and beyond.

While filming also took place in Brisbane and on the Gold Coast, Allen is firmly rooted in Coolum Beach, with the coastal community serving as the setting and inspiration for the story.

Created by Coolum local Daley Pearson, co-founder of Ludo Studio, the Brisbane-based production company behind global phenomenon Bluey, the family film brings Coolum’s beaches, landmarks and community spirit to screens around the world.

Sunshine Coast Mayor Rosanna Natoli said the Netflix launch was another significant milestone for the region’s screen industry.

“Seeing the Sunshine Coast featured in another major Netflix production proves the strength of our local screen sector and reinforces our reputation as a world-class filming destination.

“Productions like Allen create opportunities for local crew, contractors, small businesses and emerging talent while also showcasing the beauty of our region to audiences around the globe.

“Every major production helps build industry capability, supports local jobs, fosters creativity and contributes to our visitor economy.”

The production engaged Sunshine Coast crew and local residents as extras, while a range of local businesses supported filming activities throughout the project.

Sunshine Coast Council has continued to support the growth of the region’s screen industry through investment in capability development, industry partnerships and initiatives designed to attract major productions.

Long-time locals and business owners Gaye and David said they have seen firsthand what makes Coolum Beach such a wonderful place to live and visit.

“What’s made this place special to us, has always been its people, and it’s wonderful to see that spirit captured and shared with audiences around the world.

“Seeing our town, our community and familiar local faces featured in Allen is incredibly exciting.

“To see Coolum Beach featured so prominently in Allen is something locals can be really proud of, and we’re thrilled audiences will get a glimpse of the character, humour and heart that make this place so special.”

“Having known Daley for many years, it’s been an extraordinary experience to watch his success and be part of the filming process.”

“What makes Allen so authentic is that it genuinely reflects the community we know and love.”

“From recognisable local landmarks to the much-loved Coolum Kite Festival (2000-2009) that brought families together for years, the film captures pieces of coastal life that are deeply familiar to locals and showcases them on a global stage.”

“Allen shines a spotlight on the people, places and community spirit that define our town, and we can’t wait for audiences everywhere to discover a little piece of Coolum Beach for themselves.”

The release highlights the growing reputation of the Sunshine Coast as a sought-after destination for screen production, supported by skilled local crew, experienced suppliers and diverse filming locations.

President of the Sunshine Coast Screen Collective David Edgar said screen productions brought significant economic, cultural and promotional value to regions like the Sunshine Coast.

“Typically 60–80 per cent of a production’s budget is spent locally, they create jobs and support accommodation, hospitality, transport, construction and creative businesses,” Mr Edgar said.

“Productions also build local skills and industry capability while showcasing the region to national and global audiences, strengthening its profile as a place to visit, live, work and invest.”

Director of Content, Netflix ANZ, Amanda Duthie, commented in her speech at the premiere screening in Brisbane (11 November) that the audience will laugh, cry – and then google Coolum!

Visit Sunshine Coast CEO Matt Stoeckel said seeing Coolum Beach featured in a Netflix film was a fantastic opportunity to showcase the region to audiences around the world.

Allen is available now to stream globally on Netflix.

item.title: Players are Bach
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Just as they’ve been doing for almost 25 years now—usually in November–Noosa’s classical music lovers look forward to sitting back […]
item.content:encoded:
Just as they’ve been doing for almost 25 years now—usually in November–Noosa’s classical music lovers look forward to sitting back and enjoying the professional and sparkling skills of the Coast’s Pacific Chamber Players.

And this month the Players are in concert again— this time with a selection of baroque music by Telemann, Fasch, Hertel, Bach, Purcell and Handel at Cooroy Memorial Hall.

The ten musicians in the group will open with a Telemann overture which concert organiser and harpsichordist Janet Brewer describes as “playful and inventive” and followed the Johann Friedrich Fasch Concerto in C minor for 2 oboes, bassoon and strings.

“The Fasch is a trio concerto and will feature Sue Hunkin and Julia Exton (oboes) and Neil Heymink (bassoon) accompanied by Anna Moores and Melissa Buddle (violin), Andrew Paszkowski (viola), Franziska O’Connor (cello), Nik Davey (bass) and me.”

“This will be followed by Neil Heymink who will play Hertel’s Bassoon Concerto, an exciting and technically demanding work, Warren Brewer in the regal Purcell’s Trumpet Sonata and Julia Exton in Handel’s Oboe Sonata.

“Sue Hunkin will also present JS Bach’s Concerto for Cor Anglais based on the Cantata BWV 54 (Widerstehe doch der Sunde.) This will be a definite highlight of the programme.”

Pacific Chamber Players, 2.30pm Sunday November 22 at Cooroy Memorial Hall. Adults $35, concession $33 and school student $12. These are available online at www.pacificchamberplayers.com or cash at the door.

item.title: Jazz icon plays at the Majestic
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Jazz royalty returns to the Majestic Theatre, Pomona when the one and only Vince Jones visits on Sunday 22 November. […]
item.content:encoded:
Jazz royalty returns to the Majestic Theatre, Pomona when the one and only Vince Jones visits on Sunday 22 November.

Celebrating 50 years in the spotlight, songwriting, storytelling and touring Vince will deliver an intimate concert taking guests on a journey back through his career performing loved classics including Trustworthy Little Sweethearts, Nature of Power and Rainbow Cake along with tracks from his upcoming album.

A multi-ARIA recipient, acclaimed vocalist and trumpeter, Vince is one of the most beloved performers in Australian music.

Vince has carved out a singular space in the Australian musical landscape, blending cool jazz, soul and sophisticated songwriting with a lyrical honesty that speaks straight to the heart.

From his breakthrough in the early 80s, to creating 24 albums including his highest-selling album, Come in Spinner, to his enduring presence on festival stages and concert halls here and overseas, Vince has remained true to an artistic vision that’s as politically conscious as it is musically rich.

Recognised as one of the country’s most influential jazz artists, captivating audiences with his deeply expressive vocals and spirited trumpet playing, he doesn’t just interpret songs he inhabits them.

Born in Glasgow, Vince came to live in Australia at 11 years old with his family.

He grew up in Wollongong NSW, listening to his horn-playing father and singing his mother’s collection of great jazz albums.

Starting his journey at 20 years old as a bebop trumpeter playing the club circuit in Melbourne in the late 70’s and early 80’s, as a young man he had no idea that in just a few years his superb voice would touch the hearts and minds of so many.

Vince was drawn to R&B, a genre in which the emotive force of the voice is matched by technical and improvising skills.

To a young guy steeped in creativity and blessed with a sweet golden voice it was natural to meld these together and so began the evolution of one of Australia’s great vocalists.

Particular about the company he keeps, his group features elite players Matt McMahon on piano, John Mackey on tenor sax, James Hauptmann on drums and guest Ben Robertson on double bass.

Vince Jones will perform at The Majestic Theatre, Pomona from 2-4pm on Sunday 22 November.

Bookings at www.trybooking.com/au/event/1651028

item.title: Residents embrace Get Ready message
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: More than 1,700 Get Ready Noosa emergency information packs were distributed to residents at Bunnings Noosaville on Saturday 7 November. […]
item.content:encoded:
More than 1,700 Get Ready Noosa emergency information packs were distributed to residents at Bunnings Noosaville on Saturday 7 November.

Our community turned out in force to prepare for the upcoming storm and bushfire season.

The second annual Get Ready Noosa event brought together Council’s Disaster Management team and local emergency service partners, including Queensland Police Service, Queensland Ambulance Service, Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service, Noosa SES, Red Cross and Rural Fire Service.

Bunnings shoppers took the opportunity to learn how to prepare evacuation kits, get expert advice and access practical information to help keep their households, family members and pets safe during severe weather events.

Noosa Council Disaster and Disruption Public Relations Officer Ian Williams said the event highlighted the strength of local partnerships and the community’s commitment to being prepared.

“These conversations are invaluable in helping residents understand the simple steps they can take to be ready when severe weather strikes,” he said.

Council encourages residents to continue sharing preparedness information with friends, family and neighbours and to stay informed through the Noosa Disaster Dashboard at disaster.noosa.qld.gov.au

item.title: Plans for Active St alternative
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Community opposition to Noosa Council’s proposed Peregian Beach Active Street project resulted in the project being shelved in June 2026, […]
item.content:encoded:
Community opposition to Noosa Council’s proposed Peregian Beach Active Street project resulted in the project being shelved in June 2026, with at least part of state government funds acquired for the project confirmed to be diverted into other infrastructure improvements.

Council’s website described an Active Street as one that prioritised bike riders and people walking with safer pathways, bike riding-priority zones, lower speed limits, and traffic calming features.

The project was years in the planning and to be funded by grant money from the South East Queensland (SEQ) Liveability and Active Transport Funds (ATF).

Residents opposed the project through council deputations, a tabled petition, letters, submissions and at community engagement events.

Delivering a deputation to council in November last year resident Randal Delaney said the proposed project “directly contradicted the preferences of most local residents” who perceived the project as “poorly planned, overly radical, largely unwanted and failing to meet community needs” and that resident views on it had been largely disregarded.

In June, Councillors resolved to not proceed with the active street project and to determine whether available grant funding could be used to deliver practical infrastructure improvements, consistent with the priorities expressed by the community.

Council officers have received approval from SEQ Liveability to use the grant funding for a revised scope consisting of a new pathway, landscaping and way-finding but have yet to receive advice on the Active Transport Funds.

At council’s general meeting this week councillors heard the revised project scope excludes traffic calming measures, raised intersection treatments, formalised car parking, textured road surface treatments and reduced speed limit measures.

The current design instead focuses on delivering an improved off-road pathway network and

associated infrastructure, including a new concrete pathway, kerb build-outs where pathway diversions are required to avoid existing utilities, vegetation, or retaining structures, an upgrade of the existing pathway south of the Lorikeet Park bridge, verge landscaping and installation of wayfinding signage.

Subject to the approval of additional funding through the ATF, the project scope will be extended to include the renewal of the existing footbridge structure and associated substructure along the alignment and construction of a raised pedestrian crossing at the intersection of Pitta Street and Lorikeet Drive, staff told the meeting.

To avoid further delays, council officers proposed the project proceed using the approved SEQ Liveability

Fund allocation. The initial delivery scope would include construction of the pathway and associated

diversions, landscaping works, and wayfinding signage from the Lorikeet Drive cul-de-sac to Jabiru

Street, including upgrades south of the Lorikeet Park bridge.

Councillors voted on Tuesday to delay their decision on the project’s progress until Council’s ordinary meeting later this month and by which time Council officers will have conducted targeted consultation with residents directly impacted by the project.

Cr Amelia Lorentson told the meeting this would allow residents the opportunity to see the existing designs, be involved in the process and provide feedback prior to council making a decision on its progress.

item.title: Leukaemia breakthrough brings hope of better treatment
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Leukaemia doesn’t discriminate. It can affect anyone, regardless of age, gender, race or religion, which is why my mum, Jo […]
item.content:encoded:
Leukaemia doesn’t discriminate.

It can affect anyone, regardless of age, gender, race or religion, which is why my mum, Jo Jones, and I both supported the Leukaemia Foundation’s fundraising efforts.

Every year from 2011, Mum lopped her silver locks for the foundation’s World’s Greatest Shave.

Every year, except last year, when she sadly passed away.

So it’s a shame she isn’t here to read about the latest research into chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), which could bring improved treatment options and quality of life for people living with the disease.

There are more than 7000 people living with CML in Australia.

A type of blood cancer, it is caused by a genetic abnormality that fuels the growth of abnormal blood cells.

Medical advances mean that many patients can now manage the potentially life-threatening condition through medication, but only 25 per cent ever reach treatment-free remission.

But a new study led by Adelaide University and the South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (SAHMRI) has provided the first direct evidence that a breakthrough targeted therapy can rapidly and consistently suppress the molecular signals that drive CML.

The researchers compared the blocking ability of the new therapy with commonly used tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) medications, which have already helped many CML patients manage their disease for the past two decades.

“We found asciminib (the new therapy) was much more powerful at suppressing the cancer-driving protein that causes the leukaemia cells to spread,” said Associate Professor Chung Hoow Kok from Adelaide University’s Centre for Cancer Biology and SA Pathology.

“This is a huge step forward in the search for better, frontline treatment options for patients who don’t respond to current medications. Currently, 25 per cent of patients will develop a resistance or intolerance to existing treatments.”

To test the potency of the drug, researchers developed a new way to measure how effectively the treatment switches off the cancer-driving protein inside patients’ blood cells.

“Within just one week, asciminib achieved substantially stronger suppression of the cancer-driving protein than the currently available treatments,” said Adelaide University Professor Tim Hughes, who is the leader of SAHMRI’s Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia Group.

“Importantly, none of the patients experienced the poorer responses sometimes seen with the existing drugs.

“This new biological evidence from our research supports the excellent clinical outcomes from recent trials of asciminib.”

Researchers also investigated if asciminib worked in patients who had a specific genetic mutation, which is known to increase the risk of treatment failure.

They found the medication was still able to block the main driver of abnormal cell growth, but noted other factors may still affect patient outcomes.

The findings have been published in the international journal Leukemia and could help doctors identify much earlier whether a patient is responding well to treatment, allowing therapy to be tailored sooner and moving CML care closer to truly personalised medicine.

“This is an important step towards precision medicine, where treatment decisions are guided by the biology of each patient’s cancer rather than a one-size-fits-all approach,” said Associate Professor Kok.

“Our findings reinforce the importance of combining genomic testing with treatment monitoring to work out which patients may benefit from additional therapies or more frequent reviews.

“Our goal is to move beyond treating all patients in the same way. By understanding the biology of each person’s CML, we can work towards selecting the right treatment, for the right patient, at the right time.”

item.title: Happy travelling for seniors
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: “Our final guest speaker for 2026 will be Tanya Orchard who is the Business Development Manager for the National Travel […]
item.content:encoded:
“Our final guest speaker for 2026 will be Tanya Orchard who is the Business Development Manager for the National Travel Group which incorporates Trade Travel and National Seniors Travel Company,” announced Joy Fenty, President of the Tewantin Noosa Probus Club.

Tanya hails from the South Island of New Zealand but has spent half her life in Australia. She is going to share with us how Trade Travel’s over thirty years as specialists in escorted tours for the senior’s market, ensures they can offer wonderful, stress-free, travel opportunities for us.”

“I first came to Noosa in 1999 and I am delighted to be back after a covid related, longer than planned, trip back to Marlborough,” said Tanya.

“The travel industry is new to me, having worked in the wine industry for thirty years, most recently within viticulture management, but my background is distribution, sales and marketing.

I have been lucky to have travelled extensively and cannot think of another subject that makes myself and others so happy. I’m very excited to be sharing this with you.

A favourite tour has been to Vietnam. Everyone loves the food, the people and the history. It is a fabulously safe place to visit. A hands-on cooking experience and a trip to the floating markets, were the highlights for me.

Of course, I’m not biased at all, but one of my favourite places to take seniors is the South Island of New Zealand. The scenery is spectacular from the TranzAlpine train over the southern alps to the UNESCO World Heritage Milford Sound and then onto a steamship for a cruise down Lake Wakatipu.

Trade Travel is passionate about connecting mature travellers with holiday options that match their interests and needs.

We have many short stays closer to home as well as premium coach and rail tours throughout Australia – from Wildflowers in WA, to Sydney Vivid and inland Northern Territory and of course all the amazing places we have here in Queensland.

Some of my favourite ‘nearby’ places to visit include K’gari/Fraser Island and the Whitsundays – both amazing nature, scenery and we can’t forget the scenic gardens of the Hunter valley and all its great wineries….

“Internationally, I travel a lot to NZ but most recently to Europe where family and friends live in France, Germany and Italy.

I hope to get to Croatia in the next few years too, as I have heard some amazing travel reviews, and with its incredible history/architecture and scenery – it ticks all my favourites!”

“If you would like to hear more about Tanya’s Travel adventures you are welcome to join us at The Tewantin Noosa RSL on Tuesday, November 24th,” Joy invited.

“Our meetings commence with a delicious morning tea ($6) at 10 o’clock followed by the guest speaker at 10.30. Please phone Christine on 5442 7397 so that she can save you a seat.”

item.title: Hillbilly goats play Sublime
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: The Hillbilly Goats, freshly crowned 2026 Folk Band of the Year (People’s Choice, AFMA), will play Sublime Farm and Brewery […]
item.content:encoded:
The Hillbilly Goats, freshly crowned 2026 Folk Band of the Year (People’s Choice, AFMA), will play Sublime Farm and Brewery at Kia Ora, near Gympie, on Saturday 5 December.

The Hillbilly Goats received the band’s second People’s Choice award win at the Australian Folk Music Awards (AFMA), after they first took the title in 2022.

The band was also recognised at the 2020 Golden Fiddle Awards and are Golden Guitar finalists. They play bluegrass and

Appalachian mountain music on fiddle, banjo, mandolin, bass and washboard, all tied together with tight

three-part harmonies. Their high-energy, foot-stomping shows go down well with music lovers of every age.

The night is a chance to hear one of Australia’s favourite folk acts up close, in a relaxed farm-and-brewery setting in the Gympie region.

The Hillbilly Goats, made up of Fiona Passmore, Bryce Wearne and Nicki MacLucas will perform on Saturday 5 December, 7pm–10pm at Sublime Farm & Brewery, 33 Priddy Rd, Kia Ora.

Tickets: $30; concession $27.50 (pensioners and students).

Book: events.humanitix.com/the-hillbilly-goats-at-sublime

Sublime’s kitchen serves dinner on Friday and Saturday nights, 6-7.30pm. Drinks include Sublime’s own craft beer and apple cider. Tables can be reserved at sublimefarm.com.au.

For more information visit www.hillbillygoats.com.au

item.title: Investment opportunity in CBD
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: A high-performing, commercial freehold asset located in the commercial and administrative heart of Tewantin is being offered for sale. Spanning […]
item.content:encoded:
A high-performing, commercial freehold asset located in the commercial and administrative heart of Tewantin is being offered for sale.

Spanning a 1012sq m land parcel with District Centre zoning, the property at 96 Poinciana Ave is being offered by expressions of interest with Rachel Cadamy and David Brinkley of Ray White Commercial Noosa and Sunshine Coast.

It presents investors a defensive, multi-tenanted income stream underpinned by robust underlying land value and compelling future redevelopment or repositioning capability.

Positioned on Tewantin’s prime commercial strip, the property is directly adjacent to Poinciana Place/Woolworths Supermarket and down from the revitalised Royal Mail Hotel, ensuring high, continuous pedestrian traffic.

The immediate streetscape is further bolstered by a diverse mix of high-profile essential service providers, major banking institutions, medical centres and national retail brands that collectively reinforce Poinciana Ave as the precinct’s dominant commercial hub.

There are 13 dedicated on-site car parks to the property accessed by way of Blakesly Drive, and supplemented by main street median strip parking.

The centre trades strongly to an established local population, providing stable, defensive cash flow shielded from tourist seasonality.

An estimated fully let net income of $218,295.78 per annum is underpinned by a diverse, multi-tenanted service mix including a café, bakery and barber.

The agents believe the expansive freehold parcel zoned District Centre, provides robust underlying land value and flexible long-term repositioning or redevelopment potential.

“This property represents a rare chance to acquire a prime, main street asset with immediate, stable cash flow and exceptional long-term underlying land value in one of South East Queensland’s most desirable coastal precincts.’’

The property is for sale by expressions of interest closing at 4pm AEST on Friday, 4 December.

Contact: Rachel Cadamy 0455 902 627 David Brinkley 0448 594 361.

item.title: Housing market faces perfect storm
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: Australia risks turning a much-needed recovery in new housing supply into a building slump. The Real Estate Institute of Queensland […]
item.content:encoded:
Australia risks turning a much-needed recovery in new housing supply into a building slump.

The Real Estate Institute of Queensland (REIQ) has warned of a new home sales fall as major residential developers report weakening buyer demand.

New figures reported by Mirvac show it sold 429 homes in the three months to 30 September, down from 619 in the equivalent period last year, a fall of almost one-third.

It follows weakening buyer activity reported by Australia’s largest land developer Stockland.

In its September quarter update, Stockland recorded 1506 net residential lot sales, compared with 2117 a year earlier, while buyer inquiries had fallen substantially.

Australia is facing a severe housing shortage with a projected deficit of 262,000 homes against the Federal Government’s National Housing Accord target of 1.2 million new dwellings by mid-2029.

The National Housing Supply and Affordability Council estimates that 938,000 new dwellings will be built over the five-year Housing Accord period ending June 30,

REIQ CEO Antonia Mercorella said the figures should be treated as an early warning sign.

“We were finally starting to see some momentum building behind new housing supply, and now we’re seeing it rapidly lose steam,” Ms Mercorella said.

“When some of Australia’s biggest residential developers are reporting sharp falls in sales and buyer inquiries, we need to take notice. Today’s weaker demand risks becoming tomorrow’s housing shortage.”

The decline in new home inquiries and sales follow other signs of a cooling housing market.

ABS figures show the number of new dwelling loan commitments nationally fell 5.4 percent in the June quarter, with investor loans dropping 8.6 percent.

Queensland investor lending fell 10.1 percent. The total value of Australia’s residential dwelling stock fell by $34.1 billion in the June quarter, while the national mean dwelling price declined by $8,200.

Ms Mercorella said the construction slowdown was the result of a perfect storm – rising interest rates, diminished borrowing capacity and unexpected changes to property taxes.

“We are operating in an environment where uncertainty is high, and buyer confidence is low. Not surprisingly, the impact of this is that buyers are nervous about buying off the plan,” she said.

“At a time when Australia needs confidence and investment to deliver more homes, poorly thought-out policy changes risk pulling in the opposition direction.

“The danger is that measures intended to improve housing affordability and stimulate new homes have the unintended consequence of weakening investment, undermining new construction and ultimately constraining supply.”

She said the Federal Government’s plan to boost new construction by retaining negative gearing for new builds for investors was flawed because it failed to recognise the critical elements of investor confidence and choice.

“When deciding whether to commit their money to property, investors consider longer-term returns, resale value and the direction of government policy,” Ms Mercorella said.

“Trying to steer investors towards one segment of the market while making investing in established property less attractive, assumes investors will simply go where government wants them to go. In reality, some may choose not to invest in housing at all.

“A sustained contraction in new housing would have significant consequences on meeting supply targets and could create affordability issues for buyers and tenants.

“That is the unintended consequence we have been warning about, and these emerging figures should give policymakers serious pause for thought.”

item.title: Floating Land: 25 Years retrospective
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: This summer marks 25 years since the inaugural Floating Land, one of Australia’s longest-running environmental art events. Over that time, […]
item.content:encoded:
This summer marks 25 years since the inaugural Floating Land, one of Australia’s longest-running environmental art events.

Over that time, documentation of the biennale has created an enduring visual record, capturing memorable artworks and moments that have become some of the most iconic images associated with the Noosa region.

To celebrate this milestone, Noosa Regional Gallery presents a curated exhibition of photographs from each iteration of the event, accompanied by reflections on key projects that reveal the evolution, ambition and enduring impact of this significant cultural program.

Renowned for its site-responsive installations within the Noosa Biosphere, Floating Land has earned a respected place in Australia’s contemporary and environmental art landscape.

Unlike traditional outdoor sculpture exhibitions, the biennale commissions artists to create works that respond directly to place, ecology and community.

Further cementing Floating Land’s legacy, the exhibition coincides with the exclusive launch of FLOATING LAND: TWENTY-FIVE YEARS, a landmark publication exploring the history, impact and significance of the biennale.

The launch is on Friday, 27 November, from 5.30pm for the exhibition opening and exclusive book launch.

FLOATING LAND: TWENTY-FIVE YEARS opens on 28 November, 2026, and continues until 14 February, 2027.

Opening Event

Friday 27 November 2026, 5.30pm

Exhibition Dates

28 November 2026 – 14 February 2027

For more information, visit noosaregionalgallery.com.au.

item.title: Argos arrest Noosa man
item.dc:creator: Jin Hui
item.description: A 69-year-old Noosa Hinterland man has been charged with child sex offences following investigations by Argos. The man was arrested […]
item.content:encoded:
A 69-year-old Noosa Hinterland man has been charged with child sex offences following investigations by Argos.

The man was arrested yesterday afternoon when he attended a Bribie Island fast food business to meet what he believed to be, a 13-year-old girl. He was instead met with detectives from Argos.

The investigation began in September 2026, when the man made contact with a social media profile of an undercover Argos officer to arrange to meet a 13-year-old girl.

It will be alleged the man engaged in behaviour that constitutes the grooming of a child and distributing child abuse material.

The 69-year-old man was charged with using the internet to procure a child under 16 years of age with a circumstance of aggravation that the offender went to a place with the intention of meeting the child, using a carriage service to distribute child abuse material, grooming parent or caregiver of child under 16 years and possessing child exploitation material.

The man was due to appear at the Caboolture Magistrates Court today, 12 November.

Detective Inspector Sue Newton of Argos said this case highlights the risk posed to children by online predators and urged parents and caregivers to take active and ongoing measures around online safety.

“Supervision is the key to prevention, as is ongoing communication with children about how to stay safe online and the dangers of having online ‘friends’ they have never met face-to-face,” Detective Inspector Newton said.

“Our number one priority is ensuring the safety of children. Every day Argos has undercover officers working in a range of online platforms to detect and apprehend people who seek to exploit children.

“Argos investigators are committed to targeting those offenders involved in the sexual exploitation of children and the possession or distribution of child exploitation material and will use all available resources to detect and apprehend those who seek to exploit children in our community.”
